title: Optimized Randomized Hamiltonian Simulation via Average-Error Analysis
abstract: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing. Randomized Hamiltonian simulation approximates the target dynamics by sampling quantum circuits and often allows simpler circuit implementations. We develop a framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation in which Hamiltonian terms are sampled with arbitrary probabilities and the corresponding short-time evolutions are implemented sequentially. The leading channel error relative to ideal time evolution is governed by the variance of the sampled generators. Minimizing the variance-based upper bound on the worst-case error recovers qDRIFT, a leading randomized Hamiltonian simulation algorithm that samples terms in proportion to their operator norms. For typical input states, however, this sampling distribution need not be optimal. Minimizing Haar-averaged error bounds instead yields sampling probabilities proportional to the Hilbert-Schmidt norms of the terms. This choice can provide smaller average-error bounds than conventional qDRIFT. For Hamiltonians expressed as sums of Pauli strings, we combine this framework with commuting Pauli grouping to obtain smaller error bounds than conventional qDRIFT at fixed $R_z$ depth. Numerical benchmarks for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model show error-bound improvement factors consistent with linear scaling in the number of qubits. For the 108-qubit FeMoco Hamiltonian, the error bounds are reduced by a factor of about 5.65. These results establish average-error optimization as a practical design principle for randomized Hamiltonian simulation.
summary: This paper introduces an optimized framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation by shifting the focus from worst-case to average-case error analysis. It shows that sampling terms proportional to their Hilbert-Schmidt norms, especially when grouping commuting Pauli terms, yields significantly tighter error bounds than standard methods. This establishes average-error optimization as a superior, practical design principle for quantum simulation.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop optimized randomized Hamiltonian simulation techniques to accurately approximate the time evolution operator $U_t = e^{-itH}$ for quantum many-body systems.
main_result: By optimizing the sampling distribution based on minimizing Haar-averaged error bounds (using Hilbert-Schmidt norms), the authors achieve smaller error bounds than conventional methods like qDRIFT, with demonstrated improvements on large-scale Hamiltonians.
method: The core method involves deriving nonasymptotic upper bounds for the Haar-averaged infidelity and signal error, comparing worst-case (operator norm) vs. average-case (Hilbert-Schmidt norm) error analysis.
model_or_system: The simulations are applied to various quantum many-body systems, including the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and molecular electronic-structure Hamiltonians, which are represented as sums of Pauli strings.
key_observables: Haar-averaged infidelity ($	ext{r}_p(t, N)$) and average time-evolution signal error ($\varepsilon_p(t, N)$).
important_parameters: The error bounds scale with $t^2/N$ and depend on the structure of the Hamiltonian terms (e.g., $	ext{Tr}(D_p)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on deriving bounds for the mean time-evolution operator and assumes that optimizing the sampling distribution based on average error is a practical design principle.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares theoretical and numerical improvement factors ($	ext{IM}, 	ext{I}_r, 	ext{I}_{	ext{sig}}$) for both SYK and molecular Hamiltonians, showing that grouping terms leads to significant error reduction.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework for randomized simulation, contrasting worst-case vs. average-case error analysis. It then derives nonasymptotic bounds for the average error, introducing the concept of grouping Pauli terms into blocks to improve the error parameter, and finally validates these improvements using numerical benchmarks on molecular Hamiltonians.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, theoretically grounded optimization principle (average-error minimization) for a crucial quantum algorithm (Hamiltonian simulation), directly impacting the feasibility and required circuit depth for simulating complex quantum dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Improvement factors for (a) the quartic SYK model and (b) molecular electronic-structure Hamiltonians. In (a), the solid curves show the medians over 50 independent coupling realizations with J = 1 at each system size. The predicted factor IM is evaluated for n = 5, . . . , 50, while the actual-error factors Ir and Isig are evaluated for the classically tractable sizes n ≤15. In (b), IM is shown for every molecular instance, whereas Ir and Isig are evaluated through the 16-qubit NH3 instance. For both panels, tλsingle = 1 and N = 100. The dashed lines denote no improvement.

Figure 1(b) shows that grouping also improves the common error bound for every molecular Hamiltonian considered, with IM ranging from about 4 to 11. The largest improvement occurs for CH4 in the cc-pVDZ ba- sis. The variation is not monotonic in the number of qubits—in particular, the FeMoco value is below those of both cc-pVDZ instances—showing that the gain is con- trolled by the coefficient distribution within the chosen groups rather than by system size alone. For the in- stances up to 16 qubits, the actual factors Ir and Isig nearly coincide with each other and closely track IM.
